phonemes.desc: [kl], a voiceless velar stop released straight into a clear lateral — a sharp, liquid onset.
The digraph ει, by the classical period a close long [eː], held steady and bright.
Long omega [ɔ́ː] bearing the acute accent: the voice rises on the final syllable and holds it long.

pronunciation.approximation: 'kleh-OH' — two syllables; keep the first short and bright, then rise and linger on the long final ō. Not the modern 'KLY-oh'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: κλέος (kleos), 'glory, fame, that which is heard of someone' — the noun behind the name; compare κλείω, 'to proclaim, celebrate'.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *ḱlew-, 'to hear' — the same root as Sanskrit śrávas ('fame') and, through Germanic, English loud.

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Clio, adopted directly into Latin poetry without alteration.

pronunciation.note: Kleiṓ is Tier 1: the Greek original Κλειώ carries both acute stress and the long vowel ω. The restoration preserves both features — the macron marking the long ō and the acute marking the accented syllable — which the ASCII form 'Kleio' loses.

domains.title: The Proclaimer of Glory
domains.subtitle: Muse of History · Memory, Fame, and the Written Record
domains.lead: Kleiṓ is the Muse of history — in Greek terms, of ἱστορία, 'inquiry, research'. First-named of the nine daughters of Zeus and Mnēmosýnē, her name is her office: from κλέος, 'glory', she is she who proclaims fame, the power that keeps great deeds from being erased by time. In art she sits with an open scroll or a chest of books — the archive made divine.

cards.name: The Written Record
cards.desc: Her unrolled scroll — the volumen of the Roman portraits — is history itself: deeds fixed against forgetting.

cards.name: The Voice of Fame
cards.desc: To proclaim, κλείειν, is to make heard; later allegory gives her the trumpet that blows renown down the generations.

cards.name: The Archive
cards.desc: The book-chest at her feet: the memory of the world, stored, ordered, and retrievable.

symbols.name: Open scroll (volumen)
symbols.meaning: Her constant attribute in Roman Muse-sarcophagi and later art: the unrolled record of human deeds.

symbols.name: Chest of books (capsa)
symbols.meaning: The archive she guards — history as something collected, ordered, and kept.

symbols.name: Writing tablets and stylus
symbols.meaning: The instruments of the recorder; ἱστορία begins as inquiry set down in notes.

symbols.name: Laurel wreath
symbols.meaning: The crown of poet and victor alike — kleos is the immortality that song confers.

symbols.name: Trumpet of Fame
symbols.meaning: A post-classical addition to her iconography: renown proclaimed across the ages.

symbols.name: The spring Hippokrene
symbols.meaning: The 'horse's spring' on Helicon, struck open by Pēgasos' hoof, sacred to Kleiṓ and her sisters (Pausanias 9.31).

mythology.lead: Kleiṓ rarely acts in myths of her own; she is the authority behind them. Her province is not adventure but memory — the fame by which every other story survives.

myths.title: Daughter of Memory
myths.text: In the Theogony (53–62) Hesiod tells how Zeus lay with Mnēmosýnē, Memory, for nine nights, and how she bore nine daughters in Pieria 'of one mind, whose hearts are set upon song'. At 76–79 he names them, and Kleiṓ stands first: 'Κλειώ τ᾽ Εὐτέρπη τε…'. Their purpose is stated plainly (Theogony 55): they were born to be 'forgetfulness of evils and rest from cares' — memory, paradoxically, as the cure of sorrow.

myths.title: The First History
myths.text: Kleiṓ's office becomes literature in the proem of Herodotus (1.1): he publishes his ἱστορίη — literally 'inquiry, research' — 'so that the deeds of men may not be erased by time, nor the great and wondrous works of Greeks and barbarians become aklea, without glory'. The word ἀκλεᾶ is her own name negated: history exists so that κλέος survives. Cicero would later call Herodotus the father of history (De Legibus 1.5), but the Greeks had already given history a Muse.

myths.title: The Mother of Hyacinthus
myths.text: Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 1.3.3) records that Pierus of Macedon begot Hyacinthus by Kleiṓ. The beautiful youth was loved by Apollo and killed by a ricocheting discus; from his blood sprang the flower marked with the cry of lamentation. The fuller telling is Ovid's (Metamorphoses 10.162–219). A late scholastic tradition adds that Kleiṓ had mocked Aphrodítē's passion for Adōnis and was repaid with this bitter love of her own — a rare, unhappy glimpse of the Muse drawn into a story rather than telling one.

myths.title: The Invocation of the Nine
myths.text: The Orphic Hymn to the Muses (76) calls on Kleiṓ together with her eight sisters as daughters of Zeus and Mnēmosýnē, queens of the Pierian spring, and begs them to come to the initiates bringing fame and wisdom. Here the sisterhood is one power: song, memory, and the glory that outlasts death.

lore.syncretism: Rome received the Muses wholesale and gave them no new names: Kleiṓ became Clio, invoked by Latin poets and pictured on sarcophagi with her scroll. The native Camenae — Italic spring-nymphs equated with the Muses since Livius Andronicus rendered the Odyssey's 'Musa' as 'Camena' — absorbed the cult but never the individual names. In the Renaissance, Clio was lifted out of the sisterhood altogether and made the personification of History itself, book and trumpet in hand, in iconographic manuals such as Cesare Ripa's Iconologia.
lore.culturalLegacy: She is the one Muse whose name became a discipline's nickname: historians still speak of 'Clio' when they mean their craft personified. The quantitative school of history that rose in the 1960s called itself cliometrics — her name wedded to measurement. The asteroid 84 Klio, discovered in 1865, carries her into the sky, and the Clio Awards borrow her proclamation for advertising. The word 'history' itself descends from her Greek province, ἱστορία, 'inquiry'.
lore.extendedMeditation: That the Greeks made history a Muse is the fact worth pausing on: the recording of the past was not clerical work but an inspired art, daughter of Memory herself. Her parentage states a whole philosophy — Zeus begets on Mnēmosýnē the power that turns what is remembered into what is proclaimed. For κλέος was what heroes died to win, and Kleiṓ is the arbiter of it: she decides what is still heard when the generations have turned to dust. There is ambivalence in that gift, for memory selects as much as it preserves, and every archive is also an act of omission. Herodotus, her first great servant, understood this: his ἱστορίη is research in the service of fame, so that the deeds of Greeks and barbarians alike should not go aklea — ungloried, unheard.
lore.archaeology: Kleiṓ never had a sanctuary of her own; her cult is the collective cult of the Muses. Pausanias (9.29–31) walked the Valley of the Muses below Mount Helicon and describes the sacred grove, the statues of the nine, and the springs Aganippe and Hippokrene near the festival ground where the Thespians held the Mouseia. Beyond Greece, the great Mouseion of Alexandria — literally a 'shrine of the Muses' — made the sisterhood the patronesses of scholarship itself, while Roman sarcophagi identify Kleiṓ within the Muse-choir by her unrolled scroll.
